verses.text: “‘If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offerings; if he offers it from the herd, whether male or female, he shall offer it without defect before Yahweh.
He shall lay his hand on the head of his offering, and kill it at the door of the Tent of Meeting: and Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall sprinkle the blood around on the altar.
He shall offer of the sacrifice of peace offerings an offering made by fire to Yahweh; the fat that covers the innards, and all the fat that is on the innards,
and the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the loins, and the cover on the liver, with the kidneys, he shall take away.
Aaron’s sons shall burn it on the altar on the burnt offering, which is on the wood that is on the fire: it is an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.
“‘If his offering for a sacrifice of peace offerings to Yahweh is from the flock; male or female, he shall offer it without defect.
If he offers a lamb for his offering, then he shall offer it before Yahweh;
and he shall lay his hand on the head of his offering, and kill it before the Tent of Meeting: and Aaron’s sons shall sprinkle its blood around on the altar.

He shall offer from the sacrifice of peace offerings an offering made by fire to Yahweh; its fat, the entire tail fat, he shall take away close to the backbone; and the fat that covers the inwards, and all the fat that is on the inwards,
and the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the loins, and the cover on the liver, with the kidneys, he shall take away.
The priest shall burn it on the altar: it is the food of the offering made by fire to Yahweh.
“‘If his offering is a goat, then he shall offer it before Yahweh:
and he shall lay his hand on its head, and kill it before the Tent of Meeting; and the sons of Aaron shall sprinkle its blood around on the altar.
He shall offer from it as his offering, an offering made by fire to Yahweh; the fat that covers the innards, and all the fat that is on the innards,
and the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the loins, and the cover on the liver, with the kidneys, he shall take away.
The priest shall burn them on the altar: it is the food of the offering made by fire, for a pleasant aroma; all the fat is Yahweh’s.
“‘It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations in all your dwellings, that you shall eat neither fat nor blood.’”

footnotes.content: A peace offering: not for sin like the guilt, not consumed wholly like the burnt offering, but a meal shared with the Lord—and that 'without defect' speaks to something holy and free of blemish. The offerer brings the best of the herd because we honor in worship what we honor in the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hand on head, then death—the offerer takes responsibility for what is given. The priest's work at the altar began with the lay person's act; we cannot separate the people's surrender from the priests' mediation. Both draw the worshiper near.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fat covers and protects the inner workings—'the glory of the inward parts'—and here it ascends in pleasant aroma. When we offer up what shields and sustains us, we're giving the God who holds all things the honor due His name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kidneys and liver, the seats of feeling and will—the inner life—removed with care and given to the Lord. To offer these is to say, 'Take not just my meat but my deepest self, the parts that live and choose.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests kindle the altar's fire and the offering rises as 'a pleasant aroma'—the language echoes across all offerings, a reminder that fragrance itself was the ancient language of prayer, rising from earth to heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the flock now—smaller creatures, yet equally 'without defect.' The Lord accepts our gifts not by their size but by the truth they carry: that we give what is best, unblemished, whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A lamb—gentle, yielding. Its offering stands as witness that our peace with God is built on meekness, not on strength we can claim; we come as the lamb comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again the hand on the head, again the death at the tent's door—the pattern holds. Priesthood and people perform a ritual together, each with their place, both needed to make the offering whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The tail fat, specific to sheep—a generous marbling of richness. Each animal's nature is honored; the offering takes its form from creation itself, not imposed from outside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kidneys again, liver again—the holy interior. Whether herd or flock, the deepest parts ascend. We are reminded: the Lord cares for all our inward turning, our hidden selves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest burns it as 'the food of the offering'—as if the Lord sits at table with those who come. Food speaks of intimacy, of breaking bread together in covenant peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now a goat—hardy, independent, a creature that picks its own path. Yet even the strong-willed animal becomes an offering when brought before the Lord with a willing heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The pattern persists: hand, death, sprinkling of blood. By now we feel the weight of it—the offerer's act binds them to what happens, blood speaks for life, and priests are witnesses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The goat's offering rises as the herd's and the flock's before it—each creature, each kind of giver, brings the same inner fire to the Lord. In worship, we are made equal before Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kidneys and liver for the goat too—the hidden life, offered. No creature's inward depths escape the Lord's notice; He knows what stirs within us and invites us to lay it open.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: 'All the fat is Yahweh's.' We live in a world obsessed with consuming and keeping; this ancient word whispers still that our deepest nourishment belongs to God alone, and only in releasing it do we find peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Perpetual statute'—a law that stands, generation to generation, in all dwellings. Neither blood nor fat to eat: they are set apart, belonging wholly to the Lord. What is given to God is not taken back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
